# ci-manager-kubernetes

**Confirm a declared secret and converge a declared helm release in a cluster, and record what it changed.**

A forge-ci `manager` engine.

## Why it exists

A run time credential is minted by a person and never by this toolchain. The
declaration names the keys the live secret must hold and nothing else, so git
holds no secret and no value passes through a pipeline. The manager reads the
live secret and answers Kept when every declared key is there.

## Tools

| Tool | Does |
|---|---|
| `reconcile` | Confirm every declared secret, converge every declared helm release, and return who owns it. |

## By hand

```sh
echo '{"manager":"kubernetes","resources":[{"kind":"secret","name":"flux-deploy-key","spec":{"apiServer":"https://10.0.0.1:6443","namespace":"flux-system","name":"flux-deploy-key","keys":["identity","known_hosts"]}}]}' \
  | ci-manager-kubernetes reconcile
```

## In a pipeline

```yaml
engines:
  - alias: my-manager
    type: manager
    engine: "forge://github.com/alexandremahdhaoui/forge-ci/cmd/ci-manager-kubernetes@v0.1.0"
    manager: local
    spec:
      statePath: <string>
      storage: <string>
```

## Worth knowing

It knows two kinds, `secret` and `helm-release`, and it refuses any other by
name. It reads a secret and never writes one. It installs a release.

## secret

This kind is read only. Nothing in this toolchain writes a secret. The
resource name is the secret's name in the declaration. `spec.namespace` and
`spec.name` are the namespace and the name in the cluster. `spec.keys` is the
list of key names the live secret must hold, never a value and never the name
of a variable holding one, so a declaration is safe to commit and no value
passes through a run. `spec.apiServer` is the API server the declaration
expects.

The declaration is read first and the cluster is confirmed after. A
declaration that fails any check above is refused before `spec.apiServer` is
read against the live cluster. A cluster that is not the one `spec.apiServer`
names is an error carrying both, so a deploy key is never read out of the
wrong cluster.

A declaration carrying no `spec.keys`, an empty list, a value that is not a
list of strings, and a key with no name are each an error naming what was
seen. A key name that is nothing but whitespace is a key with no name, the
same way a value that is nothing but whitespace is an empty value.

Kept means the live secret exists and holds every declared key with a value
in it, and its action line names every key it confirmed. A secret missing a
declared key is an error naming the namespace, the name and every key that is
absent. A secret holding a declared key with nothing in it is a second error
naming every key that is empty. A value that is nothing but whitespace is
empty, because it exists and is as useless as one with no bytes at all. The
two are separate because a key nobody wrote and a key somebody wrote blank
are fixed differently, and a secret that exists holding an empty value is
useless rather than absent.

A secret the cluster does not hold is one error naming it, saying nothing in
this toolchain writes one, naming every declared key, and pointing at the
secret entry in the pipeline file, under `spec.mint`, for the minting steps.
There is no second shape and no branch: the manager never receives the text,
so no run log can carry it, whatever anything logs. The manager names no key
type and no product of its own, because what a secret is belongs to the
declaration that asked for it.

A dry run reads the live secret exactly as a real run does and answers the
same thing, because neither one writes. Force changes nothing here for the
same reason. Key names travel into an action line and into the three refusals
that read them, the absent secret, the missing key and the empty key. A
missing `spec.namespace` or `spec.name`, a missing `spec.apiServer`, a cluster
that is not the one `spec.apiServer` names, and a cluster that answered it
holds the secret and handed back nothing all fire before one key was read back
from the cluster, so a key name printed there would be invented. A value the
cluster holds never travels into any of them.

There is no create path, no update path and no delete path. A secret dropped
from a declaration stays as it is. It refuses a resource recorded as owned by
a different manager.

## helm-release

`spec.namespace` and `spec.name` are the namespace and the release name in
the cluster. `spec.chart`, `spec.repository` and `spec.version` name the chart
to install. `spec.values` is an optional map handed to the chart.
`spec.createNamespace` is an optional bool. `spec.apiServer` is the API server
the declaration expects. Every one of the others is required, and a missing one
is an error naming the key.

`spec.repository` is refused by name unless it starts with `oci://` or
`https://`. `spec.version` is one exact chart version written as
`major.minor.patch` with an optional leading `v`, so `2.13.0` and `v2.13.0`
are both taken. A range such as `^2.13.0` or `2.13.x` is refused by name, so
what a run installs is written in the declaration and nowhere else. The
leading `v` is dropped before the version reaches the helm client and before
it is compared to a live release, so a declaration of `v2.13.0` against a
cluster holding `2.13.0` answers Kept and names no drift. A drift text prints
the version the way the declaration wrote it, so an operator who wrote
`v2.13.0` reads `v2.13.0` back.

The declaration is read first and the cluster is confirmed after. A declaration
that fails any check above is refused before `spec.apiServer` is read against
the live cluster. A cluster that is not the one `spec.apiServer` names is an
error carrying both. A declaration therefore says which cluster it belongs to,
the same way a machine config names its node.

Kept means the release exists and is healthy. It never means the release equals
the declaration. A healthy release whose chart version differs answers Kept and
names both versions in its text, and it is never upgraded, because Flux is the
one writer of a release it already holds. A release in any status other than
`deployed` is an error naming the status, so a pending or failed release is
never retried blind. A release carrying a different chart is an error naming
both charts.

Did means the cluster held no release of that name and one was installed. An
ordinary apply installs a missing release. It is not bootstrap only.

A dry run reads the live release exactly as a real run does and answers Kept,
with the text beginning `would install` when nothing is there. It writes
nothing.

The helm client is the helm go sdk. It reads one release from helm storage in
the namespace and installs one there.

## the cluster

The cluster it reaches comes from the standard client configuration
resolution, so `KUBECONFIG`, the user's default configuration file and an
in-cluster service account each work with nothing declared here.

An install waits for the release to come up and gives up after ten minutes,
so one reconcile blocks that long at most for each release it installs. The
wait and its limit are fixed and nothing declares them.

`spec.storage` picks where helm keeps its release records. It takes
`secrets` or `memory`, and any other value is refused by name. Omit it and
it is `secrets`. The manager reads no environment variable to decide this,
because a manager runs as a grandchild process and an exported variable
reaches it with nothing in git to read. An operator who exported `memory`
would get a manager that installs into nothing and reports success, and a
declaration is refused in review instead.
